title: Fainting
summary: Fainting or about to faint: lie them down (or sit) before they fall, leg-crossing and muscle tensing if they still feel faint and have no heart attack or stroke signs, raise the legs after a faint if uninjured, and get help if they do not recover in 1 to 2 minutes or a warning sign is present.

steps.text: Check: do they respond? Are they breathing normally?
steps.detail:
Gasping or occasional breaths are not normal breathing. If you are not sure, treat it as not breathing normally.

Someone who has fainted usually comes round within about a minute (Red Cross).

ask.q: Are they unresponsive and not breathing normally?

steps.text: Are they unresponsive but breathing normally (not waking up)?
Lie them down on their back where they are, or help them sit down if they cannot lie down. Do this before they fall.
steps.detail:
AHA 2024 (Class 1): someone who feels faint should take or keep a safe position, such as sitting with help or lying down. The first aim is to stop them falling and getting hurt; about 30% of people admitted to emergency departments after fainting have an injury. Red Cross: have the person lie down on their back. Loosen tight clothing and keep them from getting cold or overheated (Red Cross).

Warning signs of a faint (AHA 2024, Red Cross): lightheadedness or dizziness, pale skin, sweating, changes in vision, weakness, a feeling they are about to faint. Some faints come with no warning at all.

If they hit their head or were hurt in a fall, use the Head injury and concussion protocol as well; if they may have hurt their neck or back, use the Neck or back (spine) injury protocol and do not move them unless you must.

steps.text: Do they have chest pain, trouble breathing, or stroke signs (face drooping, an arm drifting down, slurred speech)?
steps.detail: AHA 2024 (Class 3: Harm): do not use the muscle-tensing manoeuvres in this protocol when signs of a heart attack or stroke come with the faint feeling.

ask.q: Chest pain, trouble breathing, or stroke signs?

steps.text: Did they actually pass out (lose consciousness), even briefly?
Still feeling faint: once they are lying or sitting safely, have them cross their legs and tense the leg muscles hard. Keep it up while the faint feeling lasts.
steps.detail:
AHA 2024: once in a safe position, physical counterpressure manoeuvres (tensing muscles of the legs, arms, belly or neck) can help prevent a faint (Class 2a); leg manoeuvres may be better than arm or belly ones (Class 2b). In trials they roughly halved the risk of fainting. Effects can start within seconds, and continuous manoeuvres helped for at least 2 minutes in tilt-table tests. AHA gives them for faint feelings of vasovagal (reflex) or orthostatic (on standing up) origin.

How: Red Cross: tell the person to cross their legs and/or squeeze their leg muscles. AHA names squatting with the legs crossed as a leg manoeuvre and gripping hard with the hands as an arm one.

Do not use them if there are signs of a heart attack or stroke (AHA 2024, Class 3: Harm).

AHA 2024 (Class 2b): if there is no improvement within 1 to 2 minutes, if they faint, or if symptoms get worse or come back, activate the emergency response system.

ask.q: Within 1 to 2 minutes: are they feeling better?

steps.text: After a faint: keep them lying flat for at least 10 to 15 minutes. If they were not hurt in the fall, raise their feet about 6 to 12 inches. Turn them on their side if they vomit.
steps.warn: Do not raise the legs if they are injured, or if it causes pain or makes them feel worse.
steps.detail:
AHA 2024 (section 5.2, Class 2b): for someone in shock without injury, for example after a simple faint or dehydration, raising the feet about 6 to 12 inches (15 to 30 cm) may be reasonable while waiting for help; if it causes pain or makes them worse, lower them flat again. MedlinePlus: raise the feet about 12 inches (30 cm) above the level of the heart, keep them lying down for at least 10 to 15 minutes, preferably somewhere cool and quiet, and turn them on their side if they vomit. Red Cross does not mention raising the legs.

If they cannot lie down, sit them leaning forward with the head between the knees (MedlinePlus).

Check for injuries from the fall. A blow to the head: use the Head injury and concussion protocol.

Watch their breathing and alertness. If they stop responding and are still breathing, roll them onto their side (Recovery position protocol).

steps.text: When they feel better, let them get up slowly: sit first, then stand. Stay beside them in case they feel faint again.
steps.detail:
MedlinePlus: get up slowly from lying or sitting. If the faint feeling comes back, lie them down again; AHA 2024 says to get help if symptoms come back or get worse.

If they are hot after exertion or in hot weather, use the Heat illness (heat stroke, heat exhaustion, cramps) protocol. If they may be short of fluids (vomiting, diarrhoea, heavy sweating), use the Dehydration protocol. If they have diabetes, check for low blood sugar (Low blood sugar protocol).

steps.text: Warning signs? Fell from a height or injured, slow to come round, over 50, pregnant, diabetes, irregular or pounding heartbeat, fit-like jerking, a bitten tongue, or wet themselves.
steps.detail:
MedlinePlus lists these as reasons to call 911 after a faint: a fall from a height, especially if injured or bleeding; not becoming alert within a couple of minutes; pregnancy; age over 50; diabetes; chest pain, pressure or discomfort; a pounding or irregular heartbeat; loss of speech, vision problems or being unable to move a limb; convulsions, a tongue injury, or loss of bladder or bowel control.

Red Cross and AHA 2024: also get help if the faint feeling does not improve within 1 to 2 minutes, or comes back or gets worse.

Chest pain, trouble breathing or stroke signs at any point: use the Chest pain or heart attack protocol, or the Stroke protocol.

steps.text: Recovered: let them rest and keep an eye on them for the rest of the day. A first-ever faint, repeated faints, or new symptoms need a medical check as soon as you can arrange it.
steps.detail:
MedlinePlus: see a provider as soon as possible if you have never fainted before, faint often, or have new symptoms with fainting.

If they faint again, or the faint feeling keeps coming back, start this protocol again and treat it as needing help (AHA 2024, Red Cross: symptoms that come back or get worse).

Off-grid, whether they carry on with the trip, and whether they avoid heights, water or driving for a while, is for the group to decide with them; the sources opened give no rule for this.

steps.text: Start CPR now: use the CPR, adult protocol (or CPR, child or CPR, infant).
steps.detail:
Red Cross: if they are unresponsive and not breathing, begin CPR or compression-only CPR and use an AED if one is available.

Call 911 if you have signal. If not, send someone for help and prepare to move the casualty.

steps.text: Not waking: Call 911 if you have signal. If not, send someone for help and prepare to move the casualty. If they are not injured, roll them onto their side (Recovery position protocol).
steps.detail:
Red Cross: if they are unresponsive but breathing and not injured, call for help and place them in the recovery position. MedlinePlus: call 911 if they do not become alert within a couple of minutes.

If they may have hurt their head, neck or back in the fall, use the Head injury and concussion protocol or the Neck or back (spine) injury protocol.

Watch their breathing all the time. If they stop breathing normally, start CPR (CPR, adult protocol). Give nothing by mouth.

steps.text: Keep them lying or sitting, whichever is easier for breathing. Do not use the muscle-tensing manoeuvres. Use the Chest pain or heart attack protocol, or the Stroke protocol, now.
steps.detail:
AHA 2024 (Class 3: Harm): physical counterpressure manoeuvres are not recommended when signs of a heart attack or stroke come with the faint feeling.

Call 911 if you have signal. If not, send someone for help and prepare to move the casualty.

steps.text: Get help: Call 911 if you have signal. If not, send someone for help and prepare to move the casualty. Keep them lying down and watch their breathing.
steps.detail:
AHA 2024: activate the emergency response system if the faint feeling does not improve within 1 to 2 minutes, if they faint, or if symptoms get worse or come back. MedlinePlus: the warning signs in this protocol need a 911 call.

Keep them lying flat (raise the feet 6 to 12 inches only if they are not injured and it does not make them worse). If they vomit or stop responding but are breathing, roll them onto their side (Recovery position protocol). If they stop breathing normally, start CPR (CPR, adult protocol).

Plan their evacuation: they should not walk out alone, and should lie down at once if the faint feeling returns.

donts: Do not let someone who feels faint stay standing; lie or sit them down first.
Do not use the leg-crossing and muscle-tensing manoeuvres if there are heart attack or stroke signs (AHA 2024: harm).
Do not raise the legs of someone who is injured, or if it hurts or makes them worse (AHA 2024).
Do not let them get up quickly (MedlinePlus).
Do not give anything by mouth until they are fully awake.
evacuate: Get help (AHA 2024, Red Cross): the faint feeling does not improve within 1 to 2 minutes, they actually faint, or symptoms come back or get worse.

Get help (MedlinePlus): a fall from a height or injury, not alert within a couple of minutes, pregnancy, over 50, diabetes, chest pain, pounding or irregular heartbeat, speech, vision or limb problems, convulsions, a bitten tongue, or loss of bladder or bowel control.
Medical check as soon as you can arrange it (MedlinePlus): a first-ever faint, repeated faints, or new symptoms.
notes: Feeling faint: lie or sit down first, then cross the legs and tense the leg muscles (AHA 2024, Red Cross). Not if there are heart attack or stroke signs.
